climbing_route.label: Heather slopes to the 5,800-ft saddle
climbing_route.notes: From Lake of the Angels, climb westerly up pleasant alpine/heather slopes to a broad 5,800-ft saddle at the northeastern end of Mount Skokomish. Lingering steep snow and real avalanche exposure on the upper slopes persist well into summer, with hazard noted even in August/September.

climbing_route.label: Contour around the east and south flanks
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle a boot path/way-trail contours south and southwest across scree, grass, and rock benches around the east and south flanks of the peak, passing a large tarn.

climbing_route.label: Final scree/rock slopes to the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: Turn up to climb the final scree/rock slopes to the summit ridge. Notoriously rotten 'Olympic choss' rock and loose scree/talus on the upper mountain and summit block are the crux of the route more than any single technical move.

climbing_route.label: Southwest Glacier, climber's-right margin
climbing_route.notes: Rope up and don crampons/crevasse gear at the toe of the Southwest Glacier. The climber's-right margin offers a line of hard 30-40 degree snow/ice with relatively few crevasses, but roughly halfway up one distinctly 'inhospitable-looking' crevasse must be crossed on a marginal snowbridge - probe it carefully and be prepared for the bridge to have deteriorated depending on the season.

climbing_route.label: Loose gully to the ~8,000 ft col
climbing_route.notes: A short, steep, loose rock gully at the glacier's head tops out on the ~8,000 ft col on Spickard's southwest ridge.

climbing_route.label: Summit scramble from the col
climbing_route.notes: From the col, easy 3rd-class rock and up to ~35-40 degree snow lead to the summit ridge.

climbing_route.label: Amphitheater to the 6,225-ft summit
climbing_route.notes: From the rocky amphitheater on the west side of Mount Steel's summit, cross-country travel over heather benches and talus finishes on easy Class 2 slopes to the summit ridge and the 6,225-ft high point. Snow lingers in the amphitheater and on the upper slopes into summer, with nasty cornices reported on the summit ridge until late June, so carry an ice axe and expect firm early-morning snow before roughly early July. Water is scarce once you leave the creek for the amphitheater.

climbing_route.label: First Divide variant finish
climbing_route.notes: From the First Divide approach, follow the ridge west into a basin holding an unnamed lake, drop southwest to the saddle between Mount Steel's two summit humps, then finish north along the summit ridge; this line shares the same early-summer cornice/avalanche caution near the ridge crest.

climbing_route.label: Traverse to the west-ridge notch
climbing_route.notes: From Lake of the Angels contour/climb toward St. Peter's Gate; just before the gate, turn sharply left (south) and traverse along the base of the cliffs to a notch in Mt. Stone's west ridge.

climbing_route.label: Chimney to the first sub-summit
climbing_route.notes: Turn right at the notch and climb directly toward it, arriving at a first sub-summit rock; climb a short, low-Class-3 chimney to its top.

climbing_route.label: Exposed ridge to the summit spire
climbing_route.notes: Cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire.

climbing_route.label: Groove on the left side to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Follow a groove in the rock on the left side that bends right, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the summit. The route is Class 3 throughout (rated Grade I in the Olympic Mountains climbing guide); figure roughly 2.5 hours up from Lake of the Angels camp.

wa_northeast_buttress_4.skip_reason: The approach text stops at the base of the buttress - it describes the Colchuck Glacier approach and the moat crossing (a snow bridge or snow block that varies season to season, the technical crux of the approach) but says nothing about the 14+ pitches of climbing above.

climbing_route.label: Moat crossing and pitch to the ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: At the top of the McAllister Glacier's steep upper apron (~30°), below a line of gendarmes on Dorado Needle's northwest ridge crest, watch for a moat where the glacier meets the rock - find a safe crossing point, which can deteriorate significantly by late summer - then climb a short low-5th-class pitch to gain the ridge.

climbing_route.label: Climbers' path to the south-ridge saddle
climbing_route.notes: Watch for an unmarked climbers' path branching right (east) off the PCT toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's south ridge; take it and switchback steeply uphill for about a half mile. Many parties stash poles here for the final scramble.

climbing_route.label: Final few hundred feet to the 7,880 ft summit
climbing_route.notes: The last few hundred feet are Class 2-3 hand-and-foot scrambling on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rockfall kicked down by parties above are the main hazard on this final pitch, so avoid stacking directly below other climbers.

climbing_route.label: Into the south/southeast gully system
climbing_route.notes: Past Pinnacle Saddle you leave the maintained tread and the route becomes an unmaintained climbers'/boot path: contour or scramble east into the gully system on the peak's south/southeast face. The rock is old, variable-quality lava flow - solid in spots, rotten in others - so test holds and watch for loose blocks, especially with parties above or below.

climbing_route.label: Lower gully scree and blocky steps
climbing_route.notes: The gully starts as Class 2 scree and blocky steps. Snow or verglas can linger in the gully into July on colder years, which turns easy scrambling into a genuine hazard - an ice axe (and willingness to turn around) is worth carrying in early season.

climbing_route.label: Upper third to the summit block
climbing_route.notes: The gully steepens into sustained Class 3 scrambling with real exposure over its upper third, working through a band of trees before a final short scramble to the summit block at 6,562 ft. This route is fully exposed on an open ridge and afternoon thunderstorms build quickly over the Tatoosh in summer, so plan to be off the summit by early afternoon.
